name: Meridian Survey

stars.name: Meridian Survey A
stars.notes: A bright, young white-yellow star burning hotter than Sol; its light is hard and clean, and the system's long shadows have a blue edge that survey crews never quite stop noticing.

planets.name: Cinderline
planets.notes: A molten-skinned world kept for study of tidal heating; its lava seas are the brightest object in the system after the star itself.

planets.name: Waypoint Rock
planets.notes: An airless staging world with automated fuel caches; expedition ships land here to test equipment before committing to the rimward crossing.

planets.name: Long Meadow
planets.notes: A marginal world with thin but breathable air and hardy native scrub; flagged as a future colony reserve and left deliberately untouched pending review.

planets.name: Blue Meridian
planets.notes: A great cobalt giant whose rings are shepherded by two moonlets in perfect resonance; the system's visual signature on every long-range scope.

planets.name: Pale Court
planets.notes: A frozen giant with a nitrogen atmosphere that snows at its poles; probe teams winter instruments on its moons between expeditions.

planets.name: Halyard's End
planets.notes: The last catalogued body before the dark; its beacon marks the boundary between the surveyed Deeps and the unclaimed rimward expanse.

planets.name: The Unnumbered
planets.notes: A stray wanderer on a steep inclined orbit, probably captured; it appears on charts with no number, only a question mark, by tradition.

anomalies.name: The Far Door
anomalies.notes: A region where background starfields misalign by fractions of an arcsecond in a pattern suggesting a closed spatial fold. Probes sent through return intact, on time, and having gone nowhere. The Guild has launched forty-one. All forty-one came back.

asteroid_belts.name: The Ledger
asteroid_belts.notes: A thin icy belt catalogued down to individual comets; water here is charted property, and every chunk has a file.

stations.name: Survey Zero
stations.notes: The forward base for all rimward exploration: hangars for long-range probes, decontamination for whatever comes back, and the office where expedition reports are stamped, filed, or quietly buried.

stations.name: Cache Eleven
stations.notes: A skeleton fuel depot at the edge of the light, staffed by volunteers who serve alone or in pairs; the current keeper has been there four years and requests, annually, not to be relieved.

faction_control.notes: Chartered as an open exploration reserve under joint Guild-corporate administration: any licensed expedition may stage from Survey Zero in exchange for full data rights. Nobody holds the system because everybody needs it.

history: The system was chartered as the Deeps' final staging point when the first rimward push stalled, and every major expedition of the last century has crossed its beacons outbound.

Long Meadow was declared a colony reserve after its biosphere assays came back promising, then frozen indefinitely when two corporate sponsors began bidding for exclusive rights; the freeze is now the oldest unresolved case in the sector registry.
Eight years ago the Far Door was found, and since then Survey Zero's mandate has shifted quietly from exploration outward to explanation inward.
description: A hot white-yellow sun pours hard light across seven orbits, from a glowing cinder to a stray ice world that carries no number on any chart. The system looks like a workshop left mid-task: fuel caches, instrument winters, a reserved meadow-world waiting for colonists who keep not arriving. At its edge, past the last beacon, the starfield simply continues without permission.

Meridian Survey exists to launch things into that continuation. Eight hundred staff at Survey Zero assemble, test, and dispatch the probes and crews that define the rimward frontier, while a dozen volunteers keep Cache Eleven lit at the boundary. Traffic is thin and purposeful: supply runners, expedition convoys, and the slow return of probes that always, always come back.

That is the mystery now. The Far Door was supposed to be a way through, and forty-one probes have proven only that it is a way back: everything returns intact, on schedule, having recorded nothing but ordinary space on the other side. The Guild's report runs to four hundred pages and concludes, in effect, that the door opens onto a wall. The forty-second probe is being fitted with something other than instruments.
